| [NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda's action-readiness theory applied to impulsive action. Automatic appraisal of concern pertinence elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change a self–object relation, with control precedence. Emotions differ by mode of action readiness. Events draw several appraisals at once, and the resulting states of readiness interact, so impulse control and much emotion regulation are themselves emotional. Purposive impulsive action is grounded neurally in anticipating an action's sensory effects (PPC, premotor, cerebellum), with frontostriatal circuits for stopping. | Read |
| [NOTE-438](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-438.md) v2 | A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation | 128 experiments on interesting tasks, separate meta-analyses for free-choice behaviour and self-reported interest. Tangible rewards expected for engaging in, completing or doing well at a task undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation (d from −0.28 to −0.40), and less so self-reports; unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards do not; positive feedback enhances, except for children's free choice. The pattern fits cognitive evaluation theory and contradicts Eisenberger and Cameron's helplessness and learned-industriousness account. | Read |
| [NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Needs in SDT are innate psychological nutriments, identified functionally by the costs of their thwarting, not by individual differences in their strength. The three needs organize findings on intrinsic motivation and internalization, predict that both the "why" (autonomous vs controlled regulation) and the "what" (intrinsic vs extrinsic aspirations) of goals affect well-being, and explain need substitutes and rigid defences when needs are thwarted. | [NOTE-440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-440.md) | Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions | The authors set out nine criteria a basic psychological need must meet, separate need frustration from mere lack of satisfaction, review need frustration's costs (ill-being, compensatory behaviour, need substitutes) and propose it as transdiagnostic, review the interplay with sleep, food, sex and safety, map need-supportive and need-thwarting practices on a circumplex, and argue that the needs are universal in their effects ("output side") while the practices that satisfy them vary ("input side"). Novelty, morality and beneficence are weighed as fourth needs and not yet admitted. | Read |
| [NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | SDT's autonomy is "regulation by the self": acting with reflective endorsement, graded along the internalization continuum, compatible with external influence, dependence and a single option. Ryan and Deci align it with phenomenological and hierarchical (Frankfurt, Dworkin) accounts and use that definition to answer behaviourist, social-cognitive, reductionist, nonconscious-priming, choice-overload and cultural critiques. Autonomy lies not in being an uncaused cause but in the capacity to "reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). | Read |
| [NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md) v2 | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | SDT's canonical short statement. Social contexts that support competence, autonomy and relatedness sustain intrinsic motivation and let people internalize and integrate extrinsic regulations; controlling, rejecting or overchallenging contexts undermine intrinsic motivation and leave regulations external or introjected. Autonomy is graded: four kinds of extrinsic motivation lie on a continuum of relative autonomy (Ryan & Connell's quasi-simplex). Basic needs are defined by their consequences for well-being, and need-deprivation is offered as a principal source of distress and psychopathology. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. Will is the recursive bundling of choices by treating each as a precedent, which gives an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma and makes Kavka's toxin rational to drink. The same recursion predicts legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control, and premature satiation of appetite limits what will can do for emotional reward. | Read |
| [NOTE-446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-446.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | The paper proposes that dACC estimates the expected value of control: probability-weighted payoff of a control signal minus an intrinsic cost rising with its intensity. dACC uses that estimate to specify the identity and intensity of the control signal, which lPFC and subcortical structures (STN, LC) implement. The account unifies conflict monitoring, reward and prediction-error responses, effort costs and the override of defaults. It is a synthesis without a fitted model, and it leaves open how EVC is computed and what the cost function is. | Read |
| [NOTE-448](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-448.md) | Goal Striving, Need Satisfaction, and Longitudinal Well-Being: The Self-Concordance Model | Sheldon and Elliot's integrated model of goal striving. | [NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md) | Sophisticated Inference | Expected free energy evaluated recursively over the beliefs an agent would hold after each plausible outcome turns active inference into a pruned tree search over belief states, formally analogous to Bellman recursion. | [NOTE-463](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-463.md) | Model-based and model-free Pavlovian reward learning: Revaluation, revision, and revelation | The paper argues that Pavlovian prediction has a model-based form. That needs identity-specific prediction revalued by current state, which no model-free cache provides. It proposes "defocusing" of the predicted outcome as a model-based source of apparent habit. | [NOTE-587](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-587.md) | Pervasive negative effects of rewards on intrinsic motivation: The myth continues | The authors of the 1994 rival meta-analysis re-analyse 145 studies. They accept several of Deci, Koestner and Ryan's corrections, and code reward contingencies by what participants were told rather than by cognitive evaluation theory's categories. Result: no overall effect on free choice; enhancement on low-interest tasks; on high-interest tasks, undermining only for expected tangible rewards loosely tied to performance, or earned at less than the maximum; neutral or positive effects for rewards tied to a standard or to beating others. All of it is small. | Read |
| [NOTE-706](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-706.md) | Han et al. — From gut microbiota to host appetite | A narrative review, not systematic, by animal-nutrition scientists, of how gut-microbe metabolites and proteins may regulate host appetite. | [NOTE-949](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-949.md) | Slovic — the construction of preference | A review, from an award address, of the preference-reversal literature. Normatively equivalent elicitation procedures (choice against pricing, choice against matching) give systematically different orderings, and about 90% of reversals violate procedure invariance rather than transitivity. Two mechanisms explain them: an attribute weighs more when it is compatible with the response scale, and the prominent attribute weighs more in choice than in matching. Slovic concludes that for important, complex and unfamiliar options preferences are constructed on the spot in elicitation. The evidence is about the response under each procedure; nothing in it tests whether a constructed preference persists or changes later judgements. | Read |
| [NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md) | Flayelle et al. — A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | A narrative review and a taxonomy. Design features of six kinds of online service are linked, mostly by cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect evidence, to loss of control. They are sorted by the learning and control process each exploits. Model-free: reinforcement schedules and personalized triggers. Model-based: overvaluation, interference with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases. Providers select features by their effect on use and revenue, and personalize them under informational asymmetry. For the record it maps closely onto the parts of the potential account: features that strengthen a cue-keyed ranking, move its reference course, falsify the user's reading of progress, or pre-empt the other perspectives. | Read |
| [NOTE-1102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1102.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | A commentary. Control theory adds to goal talk the need to perceive the present state and compare it with the goal. Psychopathology arises where the loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are sensitivities to classes of goals. Valence tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value, so approach and avoidance can each produce either sign. Confidence, doubt and disengagement lie outside the loop, in expectancy-value theory. | Read |
| [NOTE-1106](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1106.md) | The Emotion Process: Event Appraisal and Component Differentiation | The evidence for the emotion process, organised by appraisal criterion and by the component appraisal drives. Appraisal criteria predict action tendencies, physiology and expression better than emotion categories do. Intrinsic valence and goal congruence have partly different signatures and combine multiplicatively. Control amplifies goal-congruence effects. Coherence among components is proposed as the mark of an episode at one threshold and of awareness at a second. No negotiation among perspectives: appraisal is a profile of criteria that drives patterned responses. | Read |
| [NOTE-1108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1108.md) | Levels of valence | A framework, not a study. Valence is located at two levels. Micro-valences are the outcomes of separate valenced appraisal checks, and they can conflict. Macro-valence is a one-dimensional integration of them and of other inputs, and it is what choice needs. The paper's work is in the paths between the levels, and above all in the integration rules, from weighted sums to lexicographic and elimination strategies that need no trade-offs. Intrinsic pleasantness and goal conduciveness are separate checks, and the paper grounds the separation in Berridge. | Read |
| [NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md) | Berridge and Robinson — Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | An invited review of the incentive-sensitization theory by its authors. 'Wanting' and 'liking' have dissociable brain systems. Drugs can sensitize the 'wanting' system so that it is lastingly hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts while 'liking' stays flat or falls. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow in abstinence, and the theory is being extended, on weak evidence, to behavioural addictions. For the record it is a mechanism for proxy-keyed potential in persons. It also shows that the addict case [CLAIM-433](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-433.md) settles holds only if the sign of valence is read along the proxy. | Read |
| [NOTE-1110](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1110.md) | Berridge and Kringelbach — Pleasure systems in the brain | A review. Reward splits into 'liking', 'wanting' and learning. 'Liking' is measured without report by taste reactivity, homologous across species, and is generated by small opioid hotspots. Dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' and leave 'liking' alone, and sensitized 'wanting' can grow while the drug becomes less pleasant. Objective 'liking' can occur without felt pleasure. For the record, this is the sharpest test so far of "valence is potential". Read as written, the identity fails, and the dissociation calls for a hedonic marker measured apart from control. | Read |
| [NOTE-1114](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1114.md) | Motivational trade-offs and modulation of nociception in bumblebees | A motivational trade-off in an insect. | [NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | A reversal of the default in dual-process models of action and emotion. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic, so they, not stimulus-driven habits or appraisal-to-action-tendency links, are the default cause of action. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and values and expectancies settle it. Emotional actions are those whose tendencies have control precedence because the goals at stake are highly valued, so emotional episodes are decision processes with higher stakes. | Read |
| [NOTE-1124](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1124.md) | Gollwitzer & Sheeran — Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis | A meta-analysis of 94 tests (1990–2003, 8,461 participants, mostly students and laboratory tasks) finds that adding an if-then plan to a goal intention raised goal attainment by d = .65 against the goal intention alone, across four problems of goal striving, with large effects on cue accessibility and on the immediacy, efficiency and non-conscious running of the planned response in small sets of tests (k = 1 to 7). | [NOTE-1131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1131.md) v2 | Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer — The when and how of planning: 642 tests of implementation intentions | A meta-analysis of 642 tests (294 reports to September 2019). | [NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md) | Future self-continuity: how conceptions of the future self transform intertemporal choice | A review, mostly of the author's own work. | [NOTE-1261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1261.md) | Generativity as a Route to Active Ageing | Two Heidelberg gerontologists read generativity, Erikson's "concern in establishing and guiding the next generation", as the psychological form of an ethical "joint responsibility" that lasts into very old age. | [NOTE-1268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1268.md) | Social Influence and Group Identity | A review of the group-identity account of social influence, grounded in self-categorization theory. | [NOTE-1282](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1282.md) | Evolution, altruism and cognitive architecture: a critique of Sober and Wilson's argument for psychological altruism | Sober and Wilson argue, from parental care, that natural selection would favour an ultimate desire for the child's welfare over hedonism, on grounds of reliability. He takes seriously the fourth: hedonism depends on beliefs linking helping to one's own feelings, and beliefs can be undermined. | [NOTE-1297](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1297.md) | I Belong, therefore, I Exist: Ingroup Identification, Ingroup Entitativity, and Ingroup Bias | One experiment, 48 Italian students. | [NOTE-1298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1298.md) | The Afterlife (Tanner Lectures I and II) | Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures. "The afterlife" is the survival of other people after one's death. Few would be indifferent to the earth's destruction thirty days after their death, or weigh its goods against its evils. Many projects would lose their point, and in an infertile world, where no one dies early but no one more is born, even enjoyments might. Humanity's survival matters to us in its own right and as a condition of other things mattering. In that respect it matters more than our own survival or our loved ones'. Scheffler reads this as our dependence on future people, not altruism toward them, and as showing that individual valuing presupposes humanity as an ongoing project. | Read |
| [NOTE-1312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1312.md) | The Concept and Psychological Consequences of Symbolic Immortality | A 1991–92 ANU master's thesis testing Rank's claim that people need to feel they transcend death, through children, an afterlife or creative work, and Lifton's two added modes, nature and experiential transcendence (a mystical expansion of the self). 440 Australians aged 18 to 88 rated vignettes as consolation in imagined terminal illness. | [NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md) | Social identity theory | A textbook chapter. Social identity is the part of the self-concept that comes from group membership "together with the value or emotional significance attached to that membership" (Tajfel 1978). Categorization is always self-relevant, and the motive for a positive social identity drives comparison with out-groups; that identity serves needs for certainty, self-esteem and meaning. Low-status members choose individual mobility, collective action or social creativity by permeability, legitimacy and stability. Identification has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. At work, identification is said to matter more than "selfish concerns" of interdependence. An imagined common in-group raised children's helping of an immigrant classmate. | Read |
| [NOTE-1316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1316.md) | The impact of place and legacy framing on climate action: A lifespan approach | 988 American adults, aged 18 to 87 and sampled evenly by age, wrote for 5–7 minutes about what they wanted future generations to remember them for (Legacy), about a place they loved and climate change (Place), or how to scramble eggs (Control).
